newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia pledges cash, notes in Soviet debt deal.
newsitem.headline: Russia pledges cash, notes in Soviet debt deal.

text.p: Russia, which has agreed on key terms of a restructuring of the former Soviet Union's uninsured trade debt, will pay 25 percent of a creditor's interest in cash and use promissory notes for the balance and the principal.

A statement issued jointly by the Russian finance ministry and 12 creditor groups said the deal provided for the restructuring of the debt on terms comparable with those previously agreed with the London and Paric Clubs.

A senior official at one coordinating bank said the deal covered some 3,000 mainly small and medium sized companies which traded with the Soviet Union until the superpower collapsed at the end of 1991.
"When the shutters came down, they were caught with open positions," the official said.
"Russia is an important market to the suppliers of goods and this must to a certain element restore some confidence."
The agreement covers creditors in Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Britain, Holland, Italy, Japan, Sweden and Switzerland.
A finance ministry official said the uninsured trade debt amounted to more than $5 billion.
The bank official said the deal covered a "substantial part" of that sum but other country groups would also come forward.
Creditors will be offered cash equal to 25 percent of a their eligible interest from January 1 1992 to the inital closing of the rescheduling.
The promissory notes, denominated in dollars and German marks and governed by English law, will be repaid in 37 unequal semi-annual instalments from 2002 to 2020, the statement said.

The dollar notes will bear interest of 5.6 percent and the mark-denominated notes of 4.6 percent between the date of issue and the end of 2001. After that both will bear interest of six-month LIBOR plus 13/16 percent.
Claims must first be reconciled by Vneshekonombank -- the former Soviet foreign trade bank now responsible for servicing Russia's debts -- and the ministry of foreign economic ties.

Russia, keen to reintegrate its economy into the financial mainstream, has already reached important debt rescheduling agreemenst with the Paris Club of sovereign creditors and the London Club of commercial banks.
Russia agreed with France last month to repay part of its Tsarist-era debt.
Moscow, in turn, wants to join the Paris Club as a creditor and officials say the trade debt deal could help.
"It is the fulfilment of the normalisation of this past problem and it will certainly be to Russia's credit," said the bank official.
